label: Person
name: Skúli Þórsteinsson
summary:
Skúli Þórsteinsson was an 11th-century Icelandic poet (skald) and warrior, grandson of the legendary Egill Skallagrímsson and a courtier of Jarl Eiríkr Hákonarson of Norway. He represents the final generation of the great skaldic tradition in Iceland before the Christianization of Norse culture changed the nature of court poetry.

A short account of his life appears at the end of Egils saga, which identifies him as the most notable of Þórsteinn Egilsson's sons. He served at the court of Eiríkr Hákonarson, one of the last great Norse jarls who ruled Norway before Óláfr Haraldsson (Saint Olaf) established Christian royal authority. As a skald, Skúli composed drápur (formal praise poems) in the complex alliterative meters that characterized court poetry — verses that praised his lord's military exploits and preserved the memory of Norse aristocratic culture.

His significance lies in his genealogical position at the intersection of the literary tradition of Egill Skallagrímsson — Iceland's greatest skald — and the political world of the Norwegian jarls. The fact that his life is recorded at all, embedded in a family saga, reflects the high cultural status of skaldic poetry in medieval Icelandic society: being a good skald was, for an Icelandic aristocrat, as important as being a good warrior.
